title: Stories of Black musicians losing their recordings and songs
summary: Johnston and Gil trade stories of demo records issued commercially without pay, and Gil says exploitation crosses color lines.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: And get paid as well for doing what you do. (LAUGHTER). Especially something that you started in the first place. (LAUGHTER). That song that Harold Arlen that made so famous and Chris Smith wrote it and he paid Chris twenty five dollars for it. I'll think of the name in a minute, but anyway, that's an unusual circumstance when he paid anything for it.
Really, I'm surprised he paid him.

That's what I'm saying. That's unusual. I know I've had jazz artists tell me that a white producer would come to them and say well we want to make a demo record and let's go do this. And they go to the studio and do it and then some weeks later one would be walking down the street and he would hear it coming out and they'd made a
commercial record of it and not one of those performers ever got a dime. Not a dime.

Well people do that to each other regardless of race, color or creed. (LAUGHTER). I mean white black people do that to each other and black people do that to each other. I mean I know one black man who bought, (one man who bought another ones composition reputedly for for, twenty five dollars and made like a million dollars off of it?).
So I mean, it can happen anyway.

It's just a general......... But a whole, what do you call it, strata, the whole strata of people who are living off a whole other thing, you know, is a whole strata of parasites. They are half middle-man-agent, half composer kind of thing you know. Where the thing goes together. It's a very tough thing to tackle.
